newsitem.title: IRAN: Iran gas potential wins over U.S. sanctions.
newsitem.headline: Iran gas potential wins over U.S. sanctions.

text.p: Iran's massive but barely tapped gas reserves can still attract a good crowd of international oil executives even with the threat of American trade sanctions hanging over foreign investment.

The lure of getting a slice of future gas export projects and an insight into the Islamic republic's plans for its reserves attracted more than 200 mainly European, executives who left Kish Island on Tuesday after a two-day gas conference.

"You ask me why I come? It's simple - Iran has the reserves and it will break out soon. When that happens the industry will change dramatically," said an European oil executive at this island, 19 kilometres (12 mile) from Iran's southern shore.

Iran's 23 trillion cubic meters of gas --the world's second largest behind Russia -- form the backbone of Tehran's plans to enter the major league of gas exporters through sales to power generators in Turkey, Pakistan, India, Europe and Asia.
Iran does not export gas in commercial quantities, dedicating its annual output of some 81 billion cubic meters (bcm) for local consumption and oilfield injection needs.

It is the large resource base that attracted foreign firms including France's Total SA, Elf Aquitaine, Royal Dutch Shell Group, Malaysia's state-oil firm Petroliam Nasional (Petronas), Australia's Broken Hill Pty Co, British Gas Agip and Gaz de France.

These firms have had talks with the state National Iranian Oil Company (NIOC) to develop Iranian gas fields -- including expansion of the mammoth South Pars field -- or play a role in overland pipeline projects to Pakistan, India and Europe.

Though no deals were signed at Kish and many of the projects are unlikely to come on stream with foreign participtation until after the next U.S. presidential elections in the year 2000, foreign interest in Iranian oil and gas potential has not been dented by the threat of retaliatory U.S. trade sanctions.
"Many of the projects are at the planning and negotiating stage but work can begin in the next two years," another executive, who also declined to be identified, said.

The Iran-Libya Sanctions Act, signed by U.S. President Bill Clinton last year, gives the president discretionary power to punish non-American firms that invest $40 million or more a year in either of the two countries' oil and gas sectors.
Clinton signed the bill citing Iran and Libya as leading sponsors of international terrorism. Iran denies the charge.

Washington's traditional allies, led by the European Union, have denounced the act's extra-territorial nature while a $23 billion gas export deal Iran secured with Turkey just weeks after the act was signed did not trigger penalties.
Exports to Turkey are scheduled to begin at the end of 1998 under a 23-year supply agreement.
Even without U.S. sanctions, Iran's gas export plans for the next decade face financial hurdles and complex inter-government negotiations over pricing, routing and security issues.

Iran plans to be exporting 4.5 bcm annually in 2000 by sales to Turkey, Armenia and Nakitchevan, rising to 41.5 bcm in 2005 by securing exports to Pakistan, Europe and Far East markets, Reza Rostami Sani, head of international projects at the National Iranian Gas Company (NIGC) told company officials.
"Foreign participation is definitely required," Sani said.
NIGC forecasts show that just construction costs for pipelines to Pakistan, Europe and a liquefied natural gas (LNG) plant for 2005 would total $16.5 billion.
